english.html: marriage <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>; and so that they succeed indifferently to all: that is to say, as much to the one who had contracted the marriage unwittingly and in good faith as to the one also who had used fraud and known of the impediment, and to the common kinsfolk also, respectively <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. And although some have rather lightly thought that such children are legitimate only with regard to the one alone who contracted through error and in good faith <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>, nevertheless this opinion has long since, and with great reason, been rejected: for it would be a thing far too ridiculous that a child should be deemed in part legitimate, and in part bastard and illegitimate <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. And as to saying that between the said du Tilh and de Rols there was no true marriage, without which children cannot be called legitimate <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>: the answer is easy, that the colour and belief of marriage, as to making the children legitimate, has the same force and the same effects as a just, true and perfect marriage <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>; as also we say that a true possession of a piece of land, or of other things, is well and justly acquired, although the delivery of that thing, and the means of the acquisition, be not real <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>, but feigned and imaginary. And if someone says here that, although this daughter is legitimate, one ought not for all that to have adjudged to her the goods of her father condemned to death, inasmuch as such a condemnation draws to itself the confiscation of goods <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>, especially in France, where he who confiscates the body confiscates the goods <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup>: I answer that although the Judge who has the power to confiscate the body, that is to say to condemn it to death, may also confiscate the goods, nevertheless one must not therefore think that he is perpetually bound to do so <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>. For such a circumstance may arise from the facts, and present itself to the judge, that he may justly not confiscate the goods, in whole or in part, and especially when there are children <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>. True it is that in France the judge must expressly declare it: for otherwise the mere favour of the children would not prevent the condemnation to death from necessarily carrying with it also the confiscation of the goods <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 23.2 (De ritu nuptiarum), the fragment beginning Qui in provincia, § 1 — not identified; cf. D. 23.2.38 § 1 and 23.2.65 § 1 (Paul), where a marriage contracted by an official in his province against the mandates becomes lawful when he lays down his office, and the children are then legitimate
notes.original: l. qui in pro uĩcia⟨alt:uicia⟩ P j. D. de ri.⟨alt:rit.⟩ nup.

notes.citation: Baldus and Salicetus (Bartholomaeus de Saliceto) on Code 5.5, l. Qui contra, cited above
notes.original: Bal. & Sali. in l qui cõtra, ia allegu.
notes.gloss: Such children succeed to both parents and to the kin of both.

notes.citation: Code 5.18 (Soluto matrimonio quemadmodum dos petatur), l. 2 as cited (cf. C. 5.18.3, as at annot-011 {f}); Accursius on Code 5.5, l. Qui contra
notes.original: l ij.⟨alt:iij.⟩ C. ſol.⟨alt:ſol⟩ mat. Accurſe⟨alt:Accurſè⟩ en lad. l. qui contra.
notes.gloss: The opinion that the children are legitimate only in respect of the parent in good faith; the Antoninus text on the woman who married a slave, discussed at annot-011.

notes.citation: Digest 40.12 (De liberali causa), the fragment beginning Duobus — not identified
notes.original: l. duobus. D. de libe. cauſ.
notes.gloss: For the rule that a status cannot be divided — one cannot be in part free and in part slave, nor a child in part legitimate.

notes.citation: Digest 1.6.6 (De his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. Filium, Ulpian)
notes.original: l filiũ. D. de iis. q ſunt ſui.
notes.gloss: Filium eum definimus, qui ex viro et uxore eius nascitur: we define a son as one born of a man and his wife — hence, the objector argues, no marriage, no legitimate child.

notes.citation: Antonius de Butrio (1338–1408) on X 4.17 (Qui filii sint legitimi), c. 2, the chapter beginning Quod nobis (X 4.17.9; as printed, ꝗ nobis), and the penultimate chapter of the title (X 4.17.14)
notes.original: Ant. Bu. an c. ij. & c. ꝗ no bis. & c. pen. q⟨alt:ꝗ⟩ fil. ſint leg.
notes.gloss: The putative marriage has the same effect as a true one for the legitimacy of the children.

notes.citation: Digest, title abbreviated de pẽca — not resolved; the fragment beginning Certe, § 1, not identified; Bartolus on Digest 2.14 (De pactis), l. Ab emptione (D. 2.14.58, Neratius), and on the same l. Certe
notes.original: l. certe. P. i. D. de pẽca, Bar to. in l ab emptione. D. de pac. & en lad. l. certe.
notes.gloss: For the acquisition of possession by a fictitious delivery.

notes.citation: Digest 28.1 (Qui testamenta facere possunt), l. Eius qui [apud hostes est], last paragraph (D. 28.1.8.4, Gaius); Digest 48.20.1 (De bonis damnatorum, l. 1, Callistratus)
notes.original: l. eius qui. P fi. D. de te ſta. l. i. D de bo. damnat,
notes.gloss: D. 48.20.1: Damnatione bona publicantur, cum aut vita adimitur aut civitas — on condemnation the goods are confiscated when life or citizenship is taken away.

notes.citation: Guillaume Benoît (Benedicti, c. 1455–1516), Repetitio on the Decretals chapter Raynutius (X 3.26.16, De testamentis), at the word et uxorem, number 836; Barthélemy de Chasseneuz (Chassanée), Commentaria in consuetudines ducatus Burgundiae, title Des confiscations
notes.original: Bened. au c Rayn. ver. & uxorẽ nõb. 836. C. baſſane. au titre des confiſ.
notes.gloss: The French maxim qui confisque le corps confisque les biens; Benoît was a judge of the Parlement of Toulouse, as Coras was.

notes.citation: Digest 5.1 (De iudiciis), the fragment beginning Non quicquid — not identified; Code 7.43 (Quomodo et quando iudex sententiam proferre debet), l. 1
notes.original: l. non quicqd. D. de iud l. i. C. quom. & quãd. iud.
notes.gloss: The judge is not bound to pronounce every consequence the law permits.

notes.citation: Code 9.49 (De bonis proscriptorum seu damnatorum), the last law (C. 9.49.10) and the Authentica Bona damnatorum inserted there; Authenticum, collatio 9, Novel 134 (Ut nulli iudicum), the § beginning Si
notes.original: l ſi. & aut. bona.⟨alt:bova.⟩ C. de bo. proſcri. P. ſi vt nulli iu. col. ix.
notes.gloss: Justinian's Novel 134.13, carried into the Code as the Authentica Bona damnatorum: the goods of a condemned man go to his descendants, and only in default of them to the fisc — the law in favour of children that Coras invokes.

notes.citation: Benoît, at the place cited above ({o})
notes.gloss: In France the judge must expressly except the goods from confiscation.

readings.reason: pro uĩcia = prouincia, the tilde marking the omitted n (l. Qui in provincia); uicia without the tilde is no word.

l. ij. C. soluto matrimonio is the number Coras gives the same law at Annotation XI (l. ij. C. ſol. marr., annot-011 note f); nothing supports iij.; Same line as p134-m2l0-1, so the same choice; ſol. and ſol are the same abbreviation of soluto with or without the point.
Accurſe is Coras's usual spelling of Accursius throughout the margins; Accurſè with a grave is a stray accent.

annot-095 note l: the same line abbreviates *qui* with the ꝗ sign (*ꝗ no bis*), so *ꝗ fil. ſint leg.* is the consistent reading; the title is *qui filii sint legitimi* (cf. note b *qui fil ſint legi.*).
bona. = the Authentica Bona damnatorum in C. de bonis proscriptorum; bova is no word.
